opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was really the core technical question for us when we started working on Glaze. Style is this incredibly slippery concept. If you ask ten artists what defines their style, you'll get ten different answers — it's brushstroke texture, color palette, how they handle light, line weight, composition choices, all of these things layered together. And none of it maps neatly onto pixels.

So rather than trying to define style ourselves, which honestly would have been a losing battle, we leaned on the models themselves. The insight was that these text-to-image models already have a learned notion of style baked into their feature space. When someone fine-tunes a model on an artist's work, the model is pulling out whatever it considers the stylistic signal. So the question became: how do we interfere with *that* specific signal without wrecking the image for human viewers?

What we did was use style transfer as a tool. We'd take the artist's image and run it through a style transfer process to produce a version of the same content rendered in a very different style — say, turning a realistic oil painting into something that looks like abstract cubism or a Van Gogh. That gives us a target point in feature space that has the same content but a different style. Then we compute a small perturbation on the original image that pushes its representation in the model's feature extractor toward that target style, while keeping the content features roughly the same.

The nice thing about that approach is it's a kind of natural disentanglement. Because the target shares the content and differs only in style, the optimization mostly moves the stylistic dimensions. We're not trying to hand-label what style is; we're letting the difference between the original and the style-transferred version define it.

And then on top of that, there's the perceptual constraint. We bound the perturbation using a perceptual similarity metric, LPIPS, rather than just a raw pixel norm, so the changes land in places the human eye is less sensitive to. That was a lot of the iteration we did with artists, actually — getting feedback on where the artifacts were acceptable and where they weren't, because artists are extremely sensitive to changes in their own work, much more so than a typical viewer.

So the end result is that, to a human, the image looks essentially the same. But to a model trying to learn from it, the artist's style reads as something quite different. When someone tries to mimic that artist, the model ends up producing outputs that drift toward the decoy style instead of the real one.

r001.rationale: The response says a style-transfer process creates a same-content, different-style version, which serves as the feature-space target for a perturbation optimized on the original image.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was really the central question when we started building Glaze. Because when people talk about "style," it's this very fuzzy, human concept, right? It's not a thing you can point to in an image. And at the same time, these diffusion models clearly learn something that lets them mimic a specific artist, so there has to be some representation of it inside the model.

The way we approached it was to not try to define style ourselves. We're computer scientists, we're not art historians. Instead, we leaned on the model itself. The intuition is that the feature extractor in these systems maps images into this latent space, and within that space, artworks by the same artist tend to cluster together, while content, the subject matter, what's actually being depicted, is sort of a separate dimension. So if you take a painting by a particular artist and you ask, what would this same piece look like in a very different style, say Van Gogh or a cubist style, and you use a style transfer model to generate that target, now you have two versions of the same content in two different styles. The difference between them in feature space is, roughly speaking, the style component.

So the perturbation we compute is one that pushes the original image, in feature space, toward that target style, while constraining the pixel-level changes to be tiny, small enough that a human looking at the piece basically can't see them. We used a perceptual metric, LPIPS, to keep that budget in check, because raw pixel distance doesn't track how people actually perceive changes.

The really important thing for us was that this was co-designed with artists. We had something like a thousand artists involved in the user studies, and we kept asking them, is this still your work, does this look acceptable to you. Because a perturbation that technically works but ruins the art is useless. Artists would never use it. And honestly, there were a lot of iterations where our first attempts produced visible artifacts, especially on flat-color or smooth-shaded pieces, and we had to dial that back.

The other subtle piece is that we had to make this robust to the fact that we don't know which model someone will train on. So we couldn't just target one feature extractor. We relied on the observation that these models, because they're all trained on similar data and similar architectures, learn surprisingly similar feature spaces, and perturbations transfer across them better than you'd expect. That's what gave us some confidence that we were actually perturbing something like "style" and not just an artifact of one particular network.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a style-transfer model generates a different-style version of the same content, then says the perturbation pushes the original image in feature space toward that target style.

astra-6.text:
The first challenge was figuring out what we meant by style. It’s easy to confuse style with content—what’s in the picture versus how the artist renders it. We wanted to affect what a model learns about the artist’s style while preserving the image as a person sees it.

So we approached it through the model’s representation of the image. The idea was to find small changes that push that representation toward a different style, while keeping the visible changes minimal. You’re trying to separate two things that don’t necessarily line up: what looks different to a human and what looks different to a machine.

That doesn’t require us to produce a complete mathematical definition of artistic style. It requires finding a way to disrupt the model’s association between an artist’s work and the stylistic features it would otherwise learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes pushing the image representation toward a different style, but does not say that a style-transferred version of the original artwork is used as the feature-space target for optimizing perturbations.

sol-6.1.text:
The tricky part is that style isn’t a single thing you can cleanly separate from the content of an image. It can show up in the colors, the texture, the brushwork, or how the artist composes a scene. So we approached it as a representation problem: could we change how a model interprets those characteristics while preserving what a human sees?

The idea is to push the image’s internal representation toward a different style, with changes that are subtle to the human eye. If someone then uses those images for training, the model gets a misleading signal about the artist’s style. We don’t need to define every element of style explicitly; we need to disrupt the association the model is trying to learn.

r001.rationale: The response says to push the image’s internal representation toward a different style, but does not explain that a style-transferred version of the original artwork is used as the feature-space target for optimizing perturbations.
